docs.title: floci-oci
docs.text:
Light, fluffy, and always free — now for Oracle Cloud

floci-oci is a fast, free, and open-source local Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) emulator built for developers who need reliable OCI services in development and CI without cost, complexity, or vendor lock-in.

It implements real OCI wire protocols so the official OCI SDKs, the OCI CLI, Terraform, and OpenTofu work unchanged against http://localhost:4599.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
docker compose up -d
curl http://localhost:4599/_floci-oci/health
oci os ns get --endpoint http://localhost:4599

See the Quick Start for details.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Contributions are welcome! floci-oci follows the same architecture and conventions as its siblings floci (AWS), floci-az and floci-gcp.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
Requirements: JDK 25, Docker (for the compat suite).

./mvnw quarkus:dev     # dev mode on port 4599
./mvnw test            # unit + integration tests
make test-java-compat  # oci-java-sdk suite against a running emulator

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
io.floci.oci
├── config/           EmulatorConfig (@ConfigMapping prefix floci-oci)
├── core/
│   ├── common/       OciException/mapper, opc-request-id filter, Ocids, OciPage, Etags,
│   │                 ServiceRegistry + self-registering ServiceDescriptor
│   ├── auth/         OCI Signature parsing (never verified)
│   ├── storage/      StorageBackend (memory/persistent/hybrid/wal), tenancy isolation
│   └── workrequest/  Shared async-operation plane
├── lifecycle/        Boot/shutdown, init hooks, /health + /_floci-oci/*
└── services/<svc>/   Controller (JAX-RS) → Service → model/Stored*.java

docs.title: Adding a new OCI service
docs.text:
1. Create services/<svc>/ with <Svc>Controller, <Svc>Service, model/
  2. The service registers its own ServiceDescriptor in an @Observes StartupEvent method, adding a service must never require a service-keyed switch in core
  3. Add <Svc>ServiceConfig { enabled(); } to EmulatorConfig.ServicesConfig + the YAML block
  4. Wire storage through StorageFactory
  5. Add the test trio: <Svc>ServiceTest (unit), <Svc>RestIntegrationTest, <Svc>DisabledRestIntegrationTest (asserts 503)
  6. Validate against the real SDK in compatibility-tests/
  7. Add docs/services/<svc>.md and the mkdocs nav entry

Never invent protocol behavior. Check the wire contract against the OCI SDK sources (the oci-go-sdk generated models are the closest thing OCI has to a machine-readable wire model).

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
AGENTS.md carries the full list. The rules worth knowing before your first PR:

  • Write explicit types. Do not use var. The concrete type at a call site is usually what a wire-contract reviewer needs to see. The one exception is a record deconstruction pattern.
  • Import the classes you use. No fully-qualified names inline, except for a genuine name collision in that file, with a comment saying what collides.
  • No wildcard imports in src/main. Static wildcards are fine in tests.
  • Never leave a catch block empty. If swallowing is correct, name the variable ignored or expected and say why in a comment.
  • Always use braces in conditionals, and use constructor injection.
  • Tests: JUnit 5 with Hamcrest and RestAssured. Name methods as a camelCase sentence or method_scenario_expectation, never testX.
  • Docs: no em-dashes. Use colons, commas, or periods.

Existing code does not yet satisfy all of these everywhere. Match the rules in code you add or change; leave unrelated cleanups for their own PR.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
• Conventional commits: feat:, fix:, perf:, docs:, chore:
  • Keep changes focused; behaviour changes come with a test
  • See AGENTS.md for the full operating rules

Please keep no more than 4 open pull requests, drafts included, and no more than 2 of them ready for review. A bot turns a 3rd ready PR back into a draft and closes new ones opened while you already have 4 open. See CONTRIBUTING.md for details.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Stable releases ship on the 15th and the last day of each month. Merging to main does not cut a release: the change rides the next train, and reaches the nightly image on the next nightly build.

Releases are cut from main by the Release Cut workflow, scheduled at 00:30 US Central time on those days (maintainers can also run it by hand). It runs semantic-release over the Conventional Commits since the last tag. That is why the commit type matters: feat: and fix: move the version, docs: and chore: do not. CHANGELOG.md is generated from those messages and is not edited by hand; a genuine correction goes in a PR carrying the changelog-edit label.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
All configuration lives under the floci-oci.* prefix; every property maps to an FLOCI_OCI_* environment variable via the standard MicroProfile Config rules (dots and dashes become underscores, uppercase).

known regions use their own realm (e.g. uk-gov-london-1 is oc4) FLOCI_OCI_DEFAULT_TENANCY_ID ocid1.tenancy.oc1..flocilocal… Tenancy used for unsigned requests FLOCI_OCI_DEFAULT_NAMESPACE floci-local Object Storage namespace FLOCI_OCI_MAX_REQUEST_SIZE 2048 Max request body size in MB FLOCI_OCI_STORAGE_MODE memory memory, persistent, hybrid, or wal FLOCI_OCI_STORAGE_PERSISTENT_PATH ./data Where persisted state is written FLOCI_OCI_AUTH_REQUIRE_SIGNATURE false Reject unsigned requests with 401. /health, /_floci-oci/* and pre-authenticated requests (/p/*) are always exempt FLOCI_OCI_TLS_ENABLED false Serve HTTPS + HTTP on the same port FLOCI_OCI_TLS_HTTPS_PORT 443 Extra HTTPS binding for clients that assume 443 (0 disables) FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_IDENTITY_ENABLED true Enable/disable Identity FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OBJECTSTORAGE_ENABLED true Enable/disable Object Storage FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_QUEUE_ENABLED true Enable/disable Queue FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_KMS_ENABLED true Enable/disable KMS (vaults, keys, crypto) FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_VAULT_ENABLED true Enable/disable Vault secrets + bundles FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_STREAMING_ENABLED true Enable/disable Streaming FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_ORGANIZATIONS_ENABLED true Enable/disable Organizations (child tenancies, organizations, links) FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_GOVERNANCERULES_ENABLED true Enable/disable Governance Rules (rules, inclusion criteria, tenancy attachments) FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_FUNCTIONS_ENABLED true Enable/disable Functions FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_FUNCTIONS_MOCK false Skip the Fn sidecar; Any other value stops startup while OKE is enabled FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_ENDPOINT_MODE host Cluster API address in endpoints.kubernetes and the kubeconfig: host (https://127.0.0.1:<hostPort>, for the Docker host) or network (the k3s sidecar's container name, for other containers on floci-oci's network; only when floci-oci runs in a container). Any other value stops startup while OKE is enabled FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 300 How long a cluster may stay CREATING before it goes FAILED FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_TOKEN_VERIFICATION known-keys How the token webhook checks generate-token signatures: known-keys (verify tokens signed with an API key uploaded to identity and map their callers through IAM; accept others as cluster-admin), strict (accept only verified tokens) or off (never verify; everyone cluster-admin). Any other value stops startup while OKE is enabled FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_LOAD_BALANCER_MODE emulated Who answers LoadBalancer Services in clusters created from now on: emulated (OCI-shaped addresses held by one appliance container per Service), servicelb (k3s's servicelb, node addresses) or off (Services stay pending). A cluster keeps the mode it was created with FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_LOAD_BALANCER_PROVISIONING_DELAY_SECONDS 0 Seconds before a load balancer's address appears in its Service's status FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_LOAD_BALANCER_PUBLIC_CIDR 192.0.2.0/24 Range of public load balancer addresses, shared by every cluster; an IPv4 block from /16 to /26 FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_LOAD_BALANCER_HOST_PORTS dynamic How each LoadBalancer Service port is published on the Docker host's 127.0.0.1: dynamic, same-as-service or none; the ports are in the Service's floci.io/load-balancer-host-ports annotation FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_PSQL_ENABLED true Enable/disable Database with PostgreSQL FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_PSQL_MOCK false Skip the PostgreSQL sidecar; DB systems become ACTIVE at once with nothing listening on their endpoint FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_PSQL_IMAGE postgres:{major}-alpine PostgreSQL image for DB system sidecars; {major} is replaced with the major of the DB system's dbVersion FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_PSQL_BASE_PORT 15432 First host port for DB system endpoints FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_PSQL_MAX_PORT 15531 Last host port for DB system endpoints FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_PSQL_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS 120 How long a DB system may take to accept connections before it goes FAILED FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_DOCKER_NETWORK – Shared Docker network for sidecar containers FLOCI_OCI_DOCKER_RESOURCE_NAMESPACE – Namespace inserted into sidecar container/volume names (floci-oci-<ns>-…) so parallel emulator instances on one Docker host don't collide FLOCI_OCI_DOCKER_ENDPOINT_MODE auto How a sidecar's published port is addressed in the endpoints returned to clients: auto (localhost when floci-oci runs on the host, the sidecar's container name when it runs in a container) or published (always the Docker daemon's host and the published port; for a remote daemon, or host-side clients of a containerised floci-oci). Only services that build their client endpoint from this setting follow it: OKE cluster endpoints do not, and are always 127.0.0.1

Per-service storage overrides use the map form:

FLOCI_OCI_STORAGE_SERVICES_OBJECTSTORAGE_MODE=wal
FLOCI_OCI_STORAGE_SERVICES_OBJECTSTORAGE_FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS=5000

docs.title: Resource identity labels
docs.text:
Every container and volume floci-oci creates carries the base labels floci=true, floci_emulator=floci-oci and, when FLOCI_OCI_DOCKER_RESOURCE_NAMESPACE is set, floci_namespace. Function containers that fnserver starts itself are not labelled. A container backing an emulated OCI resource also carries labels tying it back to that resource, additive to the base labels:

Label Value Purpose io.floci oci Cloud provider, for multi-cloud discovery when several Floci emulators share a host io.floci.service e.g. oke The OCI service the container backs io.floci.resource-id e.g. ocid1.cluster.oc1.iad.… The resource OCID, as the OCI CLI and SDKs take it io.floci.compartment the compartment OCID The compartment the resource belongs to io.floci.region e.g. us-ashburn-1 The region the resource belongs to (an OKE cluster's own region). The shared Fn server serves every region and carries no region label floci_service same value as io.floci.service Legacy alias, written alongside io.floci.service; prefer the new key

This makes docker ps --filter label=io.floci.resource-id=<cluster-ocid> resolve an emulated resource to its backing container directly. Applied to Container Engine (OKE) clusters and Functions. The Functions fnserver container is a shared singleton serving every application, so it carries every label except io.floci.resource-id and io.floci.compartment.

The io.floci.* key set is shared with floci-aws, floci-gcp and floci-az, so docker ps --filter label=io.floci lists every resource-backing container on a shared host.

docs.title: Initialization Hooks
docs.text:
floci-oci runs shell scripts from lifecycle-phase directories, mirroring the other Floci emulators.

Phase Directory When boot /etc/floci-oci/init/boot.d Before services initialize — OCI APIs are not available yet start /etc/floci-oci/init/start.d After the HTTP server is listening ready /etc/floci-oci/init/ready.d After start hooks complete shutdown /etc/floci-oci/init/stop.d (or shutdown.d) On graceful shutdown

Scripts run in lexicographic order. A failing start/ready script aborts startup.

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  floci-oci:
    volumes:
      - ./init-scripts:/etc/floci-oci/init/ready.d

#!/bin/sh
# init-scripts/10-create-bucket.sh
oci os bucket create --endpoint http://localhost:4599 \
  --compartment-id "$FLOCI_OCI_DEFAULT_TENANCY_ID" \
  --namespace floci-local --name seeded-bucket

Hook state is inspectable at GET /_floci-oci/init.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Property Default Description floci-oci.init-hooks.shell-executable /bin/sh Interpreter for hook scripts floci-oci.init-hooks.timeout-seconds 30 Per-script timeout floci-oci.init-hooks.shutdown-grace-period-seconds 2 Grace period for shutdown hooks

docs.title: Storage Modes
docs.text:
floci-oci supports four storage modes, selected globally with floci-oci.storage.mode (FLOCI_OCI_STORAGE_MODE) and overridable per service.

Mode Behaviour Use case memory (default) Everything in memory, lost on restart Fast tests, CI persistent Write-through JSON files on every change Durability over speed hybrid In-memory with periodic flush to disk Balanced local development wal Write-ahead log + periodic snapshot compaction Durability with fast writes

Persistent state is written under floci-oci.storage.persistent-path (default ./data, /app/data in the Docker image — mount a volume to keep it).

docs.title: Per-service overrides
docs.text:
floci-oci:
  storage:
    mode: memory
    services:
      objectstorage:
        mode: wal
        flush-interval-ms: 5000

docs.title: Multi-tenancy
docs.text: Every storage key is transparently prefixed with the calling tenancy's OCID, so requests signed with different tenancy OCIDs see fully isolated resources.

docs.title: OCI CLI & SDK Setup
docs.text: floci-oci parses the OCI request signature for tenancy/user context but never verifies the RSA signature: any locally generated API key works. No account, no real credentials. The one exception is OKE: kubectl tokens signed with a key you upload to identity (oci iam user api-key upload) are verified and their caller mapped through IAM, as on OKE.

docs.title: OCI CLI
docs.text:
Create a throwaway key and config once:

mkdir -p ~/.oci
openssl genrsa -out ~/.oci/floci_key.pem 2048

cat > ~/.oci/config <<'EOF'
[FLOCI]
user=ocid1.user.oc1..flocilocaluser0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000
fingerprint=aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff:00:11:22:33:44:55:66:77:88:99
tenancy=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..flocilocaltenancy0000000000000000000000000000000000000000
region=us-ashburn-1
key_file=~/.oci/floci_key.pem
EOF

Then point the CLI at the emulator:

oci --profile FLOCI os ns get --endpoint http://localhost:4599

docs.text:

docs.title: Multi-tenancy
docs.text: The tenancy OCID in your signing key's keyId is the storage partition — requests signed with different tenancy OCIDs see isolated resources. Session auth (--auth security_token) signs with a ST$<token> keyId instead; its tenancy is the token's tenant claim, read without verifying the token. Unsigned requests fall back to the configured floci-oci.default-tenancy-id.

docs.title: Regions
docs.text:
Regional resources (buckets, queues, streams, vaults, keys, secrets, functions, clusters) are partitioned by region as well as tenancy. The region comes from the request Host header: the first dot-separated label that is a known OCI region name, so any host that names a region works in it. The simplest way to send one is the public wildcard <service>.<region>.localhost.floci.io, which resolves to 127.0.0.1: for example http://messaging.us-phoenix-1.localhost.floci.io:4599 works in us-phoenix-1. Any other host, such as localhost:4599, reaches the tenancy's home region. Regional OCIDs carry the three letter region key (ocid1.queue.oc1.phx.…), as real Object Storage bucket OCIDs do; some newer OCI services use the full region name there instead.

Identity is global, as on real OCI: compartments, users, groups and policies are shared by every region of the tenancy. Each tenancy has its own home region: a tenancy seen for the first time gets default-region, and keeps it if default-region changes later. As on real OCI, Identity writes are only accepted at the home region (403 NotAllowed elsewhere), and a tenancy can only use a region it is subscribed to (401 NotAuthenticated otherwise): the home region always is, and CreateRegionSubscription adds another at once. See Identity for the details.

Data persisted by an older floci-oci, before region partitioning, is moved into default-region on startup.

docs.title: Wire contract
docs.text:
Every service follows the OCI wire contract:

  • Errors are {"code": "...", "message": "..."} with the correct HTTP status; missing resources report 404 NotAuthorizedOrNotFound exactly as real OCI does.
  • Every response carries an opc-request-id header (echoing yours if provided), and opc-client-request-id is echoed back.
  • Lists paginate via limit/page query parameters and the opc-next-page response header. Identity lists return bare JSON arrays.
  • Mutations carry etag headers and honour if-match / if-none-match.
  • Async operations return 202 + opc-work-request-id, pollable via the work-request endpoints.

docs.title: Kubernetes Versions
docs.text:
floci-oci offers the versions OKE supports, as listed in Oracle's release calendar on 2026-11-10 (Supported Versions of Kubernetes), each pinned to the k3s image of the same patch (<image-repository>:v<version>-k3s1, image-repository defaults to rancher/k3s):

Version k3s image OKE status v1.34.10 rancher/k3s:v1.34.10-k3s1 supported v1.35.0 rancher/k3s:v1.35.0-k3s1 preview v1.35.2 rancher/k3s:v1.35.2-k3s1 supported v1.36.4 rancher/k3s:v1.36.4-k3s1 supported, newest v1.37.0 rancher/k3s:v1.37.0-k3s1 preview
  • Creating a cluster: kubernetesVersion is required, as in the SDK (400 MissingParameter without it) and must be one of the versions above (400 InvalidParameter otherwise). Versions OKE has retired, such as the v1.28.2 and v1.29.1 older floci-oci builds advertised, are refused.
  • Options: GetClusterOptions and GetNodePoolOptions with all list the newest patch of each minor plus the previews; shouldListAllPatchVersions=true lists every patch. With a cluster OCID, cluster options list the cluster's version and the versions it can be upgraded to, and node pool options list the versions a node pool of that cluster may run. nodePoolOptions also lists the shapes in the catalog below.
  • Upgrading the control plane: UpdateCluster with a newer kubernetesVersion recreates the k3s server on the new image, on the same volume, so the cluster keeps its data, its CA and its nodes. The cluster is UPDATING with an IN_PROGRESS CLUSTER_UPDATE work request until the new server answers /readyz, then ACTIVE. "Kubernetes requires that you upgrade control plane nodes one minor version at a time", there is no downgrade, and every node pool version and node version must stay within three minor versions (Kubernetes Versions and Kubernetes Engine, Upgrading the control plane); any other target is 400 InvalidParameter. availableKubernetesUpgrades lists the supported versions newer than the cluster's, up to the next minor. Worker nodes are not upgraded with the control plane.
  • Node pool versions: a node pool's kubernetesVersion (default: the cluster's) must not be newer than the control plane nor more than three minor versions behind it ("The worker nodes in a cluster must not run a more recent version of Kubernetes than the associated control plane nodes", upgrade overview). "Changing the Kubernetes version configured for a managed node pool does not change the Kubernetes version running on existing managed nodes" (same page): existing nodes keep theirs and new nodes take the pool's.
  • Node cycling: with nodePoolCyclingDetails.isNodeCyclingEnabled, a version change replaces the nodes (Upgrading worker nodes). cycleModes INSTANCE_REPLACE (floci-oci's default, as the SDK states none) gives every node a new instance, OCID and address; BOOT_VOLUME_REPLACE keeps each node's instance, address and name and restarts it on the new version. floci-oci replaces all nodes at once rather than maximumSurge and maximumUnavailable at a time, and does not cordon or drain them first.
  • Clusters stored by an older floci-oci on a version it no longer offers keep running on the image they ran on before (rancher/k3s:v1.30.1-k3s1), without that version being advertised.

docs.title: Real-Mode Runtime
docs.text: When real mode is enabled (FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_MOCK=false, the default outside tests), each cluster is a set of Docker containers on its own Docker network.

docs.title: Control plane
docs.text:
• Agentless k3s server: the server runs k3s server --disable-agent --egress-selector-mode=cluster, so it runs no kubelet and reaches the kubelets and pods through the agents' tunnels. kubectl get nodes lists only the worker nodes, and answers "No resources found" before the first node pool, as on OKE (Oracle's vLLM on OKE tutorial shows both). traefik, local-storage and metrics-server are disabled (see Storage and Add-ons).
  • Cluster network: the server and its agents share the Docker network floci-oci-oke-net-<cluster OCID>, created with the cluster and removed on delete, with a 10.0.X.0/24 subnet starting at 10.0.10.0/24 (the worker subnet of OKE's quick-create workflow), skipping subnets other Docker networks hold or that overlap the cluster's pod or service network. Agents find the server by container name on it. The server is also attached to floci-oci's own network (or FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_DOCKER_NETWORK), so the token webhook and in-Docker clients keep working.
  • Lifecycle: CreateCluster returns the cluster CREATING with an IN_PROGRESS work request. floci-oci polls the k3s API in the background; once /readyz answers, the cluster becomes ACTIVE and the work request SUCCEEDED, whatever the number of nodes. This is what Terraform and oci ce cluster create --wait-for-state wait on. A server that exits, or an API that is not ready within FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_READY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (default 300), marks both FAILED.
  • Dynamic Port Allocation: Each cluster's Kubernetes API server is bound to a dynamic host port in the configured range (default: 6443..6543). The port is published on all host interfaces, so the API is reachable from other machines that can reach the host.
  • Reaching the API from other containers: by default (FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_ENDPOINT_MODE=host) endpoints.kubernetes and the kubeconfig server are https://127.0.0.1:<hostPort>, which a client in another container cannot reach. Set FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_ENDPOINT_MODE=network when floci-oci runs in a container (as in docker-compose.yml) and the clients are containers on the same Docker network: the address becomes https://<sidecar container name>:6443, for example https://floci-oci-oke-ocid1.cluster.oc1.iad.<unique>:6443. Every sidecar's serving certificate carries its container name as a SAN, so TLS still verifies against the kubeconfig CA. When floci-oci runs on the host, network falls back to host, as floci-aws EKS does. It also falls back, with a warning in the log, when the sidecar's network is Docker's default bridge (or host, none), since those networks have no container-name lookup: run floci-oci on a user-defined network, as docker-compose.yml does, or set FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_DOCKER_NETWORK to one. The container name contains dots and can have a label that starts with a digit: kubectl and other Go clients accept it, but Java's java.net.URI does not parse it as a host.

docs.title: Node pools as nodes
docs.text:
• One k3s agent per node: every node of a node pool is a k3s agent container (floci-oci-oke-node-<instance OCID>) at a fixed address of the cluster network, from .16 up, with its own named volume. A node pool is CREATING (or UPDATING after a change that adds or replaces nodes) with an IN_PROGRESS work request until all its nodes are Ready, then ACTIVE; a pool with no node is ACTIVE at once. Nodes not Ready within the ready timeout make the pool FAILED.
  • How many nodes, and where: nodeConfigDetails.size spread over nodeConfigDetails.placementConfigs in turn, else the deprecated quantityPerSubnet nodes in each of subnetIds (oci-go-sdk CreateNodePoolDetails). Nodes go to the placement's faultDomains in turn, else to FAULT-DOMAIN-1 to -3 of their availability domain in turn ("Each availability domain has three fault domains", Supported Labels). UpdateNodePool with a new size, placement or subnet list adds or removes nodes; a smaller pool removes its newest nodes first. Removing a node stops its agent, deletes its Kubernetes Node object and its volume.
  • Node cap: at most FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_MAX_NODES_PER_CLUSTER (default 5) agents run per cluster, given to node pools in creation order. Nodes past the cap still appear in GetNodePool as ACTIVE, with a lifecycleDetails note and no Kubernetes node, and a WARN names the cap and the pools short of nodes. The API always reports the requested counts.
  • Shapes and sizing: each agent container is limited to its shape's CPUs and memory (at most four fifths of the Docker host's memory and all its CPUs), and the kubelet reserves the rest of the host, so a node's allocatable resources come close to its shape. Fixed shapes take Oracle's sizes; flexible shapes take nodeShapeConfig.ocpus and memoryInGBs within the shape's limits, where memory runs from "1 GB or a value matching the number of OCPUs, whichever is greater" to "64 GB per OCPU" up to the shape's maximum (Compute Shapes); out-of-range values are 400 InvalidParameter. An x86 OCPU is two vCPUs, an Ampere A1 OCPU one. Oracle does not document OKE's defaults when nodeShapeConfig is partial: floci-oci uses 1 OCPU and 16 GB per OCPU (6 GB on VM.Standard.A1.Flex). A shape outside the catalog is accepted and sized as 1 OCPU with 16 GB.
Shapes Sizes (Compute Shapes) Fixed VM.Standard2.1/.2/.4/.8, VM.Standard.E2.1, VM.Standard.E2.2, VM.Standard.E2.1.Micro Flexible VM.Standard.E3.Flex, VM.Standard.E4.Flex (64 OCPUs, 1024 GB), VM.Standard.E5.Flex (126 OCPUs, 1049 GB), VM.Standard3.Flex (32, 512), VM.Optimized3.Flex (18, 256), VM.Standard.A1.Flex (76, 472), VM.Standard.A2.Flex (78, 946) GPU VM.GPU2.1, VM.GPU3.1/.2/.4, VM.GPU.A10.1/.2, BM.GPU2.2, BM.GPU3.8, BM.GPU4.8, BM.GPU.A10.4, BM.GPU.A100-v2.8, BM.GPU.H100.8, BM.GPU.H200.8, BM.GPU.L40S.4, BM.GPU.B200.8
  • GPU shapes: a node of a GPU shape registers with the taint OKE GPU nodes carry, nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule ("OKE GPU nodes have a nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule taint", vLLM on OKE), and advertises the shape's GPU count as nvidia.com/gpu capacity and allocatable, so a pod that requests GPUs and tolerates the taint schedules on it. On OKE the NVIDIA device plugin advertises the GPUs; here floci-oci sets the capacity on the node status, there is no GPU and no device plugin, and a container that needs a real GPU will not find one.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
k3s starts with --disable=local-storage, and every cluster gets the two storage classes OKE defines, from k3s's auto-deploy directory: "Two storage classes are defined by default, oci-bv for the CSI volume plugin and oci for the FlexVolume plugin", and in clusters created on Kubernetes 1.24 or later "the oci-bv storage class is initially set as the default" (Provisioning PVCs on the Block Volume service). Their definitions follow oracle/oci-cloud-controller-manager's manifests/container-storage-interface/storage-class.yaml and manifests/volume-provisioner/storage-class.yaml:

StorageClass Provisioner Default Binding mode Expansion oci-bv blockvolume.csi.oraclecloud.com yes WaitForFirstConsumer yes oci oracle.com/oci no Immediate no

Each class is served by a local-path-provisioner instance registered under that provisioner name, so PVCs bind and PVs carry pv.kubernetes.io/provisioned-by: blockvolume.csi.oraclecloud.com. oci-bv volumes live on the node that first uses them; oci volumes bind before any node is chosen, so they live on a volume every agent of the cluster mounts. Not emulated: OKE's 50 GB minimum and rounding of PVC sizes, block volume performance, encryption and the oci-bv-encrypted class the CCM manifests also define (OKE does not create it by default).

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
• Pod and service networks: from options.kubernetesNetworkConfig.podsCidr and servicesCidr, defaulting to 10.244.0.0/16 and 10.96.0.0/16 (oci-go-sdk KubernetesNetworkConfig: "Optional, defaults to 10.244.0.0/16" and "defaults to 10.96.0.0/16"). Each node takes a /25 of the pod network: "Kubernetes Engine allocates a /25 CIDR block of network addresses for each worker node in a cluster" (IPv4 CIDR Blocks and Kubernetes Engine). The cluster DNS service (kube-dns) sits at 10.96.5.5 in the default service network, as Oracle's Cilium on OKE tutorial shows; in another service network floci-oci takes the same offset when it fits, else the tenth address.
  • Validation: both must be IPv4 CIDR blocks between /8 and /28 that do not overlap ("must not overlap", CIDR blocks), and the pod network must hold at least one /25; otherwise 400 InvalidParameter. Oracle documents no error code or size limit for these cases, so both are floci-oci's choice.
  • CNI: k3s's flannel runs whatever clusterPodNetworkOptions.cniType says. OCI_VCN_IP_NATIVE (pods taking addresses from a VCN subnet) is stored and echoed but not emulated.

docs.title: LoadBalancer Services
docs.text:
On OKE, a Service of type LoadBalancer gets an OCI Load Balancer (the default) or, with oci.oraclecloud.com/load-balancer-type: "nlb", an OCI Network Load Balancer, created by OKE's cloud controller manager; "The load balancer may take a few minutes to go from a pending state to being fully operational", and its address appears as the Service's EXTERNAL-IP, for example 192.0.2.22 (Provisioning OCI Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers). floci-oci emulates that controller for clusters created in real mode (FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_LOAD_BALANCER_MODE=emulated, the default): k3s's own servicelb is off (--disable=servicelb) and floci-oci writes the OCI-shaped address into the Service's status.

  • Which Services: those of type LoadBalancer without spec.loadBalancerClass, the ones a cloud controller handles (kubernetes/cloud-provider wantsLoadBalancer); a Service with a class is left to whatever implements it.
  • Addresses: a public load balancer takes an address from 192.0.2.0/24 (FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_LOAD_BALANCER_PUBLIC_CIDR, RFC 5737's TEST-NET-1, the range of Oracle's own example, never routed), unique across every cluster of the emulator, from .10 up. An internal one (service.beta.kubernetes.io/oci-load-balancer-internal: "true", or for an NLB oci-network-load-balancer.oraclecloud.com/internal: "true") takes an address of the cluster's node subnet from .254 down; node addresses go from .16 up and the two never meet. spec.loadBalancerIP (a reserved public IP on OKE) is honored when it is a free address of the public range; oci-network-load-balancer.oraclecloud.com/assigned-private-ipv4 when it is a free address of the node subnet. Addresses are stored, so they survive a restart.
  • Status (loadBalancerToStatus in oracle/oci-cloud-controller-manager): one ingress entry per address the load balancer has. A public OCI Load Balancer has its public address; an internal one its private address; a public NLB has a private and a public address (private first), or only the public one with oci-network-load-balancer.oraclecloud.com/external-ip-only: "true". oci.oraclecloud.com/ingress-ip-mode: Proxy|VIP sets ipMode.
  • Refused as the CCM refuses them, with a SyncLoadBalancerFailed Warning event and the Service left <pending>: UDP on an OCI Load Balancer ("OCI load balancers do not support UDP"; use an NLB), UDP on an NLB whose security list management mode is not None, sessionAffinity other than None, oci-load-balancer-shape: flexible without -shape-flex-min and -shape-flex-max, an invalid boolean or ingress-ip-mode, loadBalancerIP on an internal load balancer, assigned-private-ipv4 on an OCI Load Balancer, and an address floci-oci cannot give (outside the range, or taken).
  • Lifecycle, as a cloud controller does it: the service.kubernetes.io/load-balancer-cleanup finalizer is added first, the events EnsuringLoadBalancer, EnsuredLoadBalancer, UpdatedLoadBalancer (backends changed), UnAvailableLoadBalancer (no backend), DeletingLoadBalancer and DeletedLoadBalancer are recorded from service-controller with the upstream messages, and when the Service is deleted or stops being a LoadBalancer the address is released, its appliance removed and the finalizer dropped last. FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_LOAD_BALANCER_PROVISIONING_DELAY_SECONDS (default 0) holds the status back to mimic OKE's "few minutes".
  • Data path: each load balancer is an appliance container (floci-oci-oke-lb-<Service UID>) started from the cluster's own k3s image, with NET_ADMIN and IP forwarding but not privileged, that holds the load balancer's addresses and forwards each Service port to the NodePort of the backend nodes, picked at random, masquerading the source. The backends are the Ready nodes of the cluster's node pools not labelled node.kubernetes.io/exclude-from-external-load-balancers; with externalTrafficPolicy: Local, only those with a ready endpoint of the Service. An internal appliance sits on the cluster network at its address; a public one on the Docker network floci-oci-oke-lb-public (created with the first public load balancer, removed with the last) at its public address, joined to the cluster network to reach the nodes. Every appliance also joins floci-oci's own network when floci-oci runs in a container. loadBalancerSourceRanges (IPv4) limits who is forwarded.
  • Host ports: each Service port is also published on the Docker host's 127.0.0.1, at a free port by default (FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_LOAD_BALANCER_HOST_PORTS=dynamic), at the Service's own port with same-as-service (a free port when it is taken), or not at all with none. The ports are written on the Service as the annotation floci.io/load-balancer-host-ports, for example TCP/80=127.0.0.1:32768, and kept when the appliance is replaced.
From Internal address Public address A pod of the cluster yes (kube-proxy, and the appliance) yes (kube-proxy) A container on the cluster's network yes only when also on floci-oci-oke-lb-public A container on floci-oci's network the appliance by name or its address on that network same The Docker host (macOS included) 127.0.0.1:<host port> same A Linux Docker host also the address itself also the address itself
  • Modes: servicelb keeps k3s's servicelb, which publishes the node addresses as before; off disables it and leaves Services <pending>. A cluster keeps the mode it was created with: a cluster stored by an earlier floci-oci, which had servicelb, keeps it when it is restored, so its Services keep their addresses (recreate the cluster to move it).
  • Not emulated: OCI Load Balancer and Network Load Balancer resources (floci-oci has no Load Balancer service, so nothing appears in the OCI API, and serviceLbSubnetIds and serviceLbConfig are only echoed), real public addresses, shapes and bandwidth, health checks and backend policies, TLS listeners, security lists and NSGs, node-label-selector, client source address preservation (the appliance masquerades), allocateLoadBalancerNodePorts: false (no NodePort to forward to; the address is still reported), and IPv6.
  • Not verified: that a public NLB reports a private and a public address, and in which order (inferred from the CCM code); publishing an appliance's ports on Docker Desktop or colima (verified on Linux Docker only); real provisioning times.

docs.title: Cluster add-ons
docs.text:
• Defaults: OKE deploys the Kubernetes Metrics Server only as an optional add-on, and "Optional cluster add-ons are not deployed by default" (Overview of Cluster Add-ons). So k3s's bundled metrics-server is disabled and kubectl top fails until the KubernetesMetricsServer add-on is installed.
  • Offered add-ons: KubernetesMetricsServer, which deploys metrics-server (rancher/mirrored-metrics-server:v0.8.1, Deployment metrics-server in kube-system, as on OKE), and CertManager, which is recorded but deploys nothing. "To use the Kubernetes Metrics Server as a cluster add-on, you also have to deploy cert-manager", or set the skipAddonDependenciesCheck configuration to true when cert-manager runs standalone (Kubernetes Metrics Server as a Cluster Add-on). Other OKE add-ons are not offered (404 NotAuthorizedOrNotFound).
  • Rules: "You can only configure cluster add-ons when using enhanced clusters" (Configuring Cluster Add-ons); on a basic cluster add-ons are 400 InvalidParameter. A cluster created without type is a basic cluster, as OKE creates one through the CLI or API until June 15, 2027 (OKE service change announcement), so add-ons need type: ENHANCED_CLUSTER. InstallAddon of an installed add-on without isOverrideExisting is 409 Conflict, and the missing dependency 400 InvalidParameter; Oracle documents neither error, so both are floci-oci's choice. DisableAddon needs isRemoveExistingAddOn, which with true also removes what the add-on deployed. Each operation answers 202 with an ENABLE_ADDON, UPDATE_ADDON or DISABLE_ADDON work request. ListAddonOptions needs kubernetesVersion. The add-on versions are the components floci-oci deploys, not OKE's.
  • Persistence: metrics-server's manifest lives on the server's volume, so it survives a control plane upgrade and a restart.

docs.title: Restore at startup
docs.text: In persistent, hybrid or wal storage modes, floci-oci restores every stored cluster at startup: it adopts a surviving server (matched by container name, labels, image and flags) or recreates it on the surviving volume, keeping its CA; when the volume is gone it starts a fresh server and logs that the CA changed. It then adopts each node's agent (matched by labels, image, server address and join token), recreates missing ones, and removes agents no node of the cluster has. Node pools stored before nodes were run get their agents then. Load balancers keep their stored addresses; the first controller pass adopts each appliance that still runs with the same configuration and recreates the others. In memory mode nothing is restored. Clusters stored by an older floci-oci restart on the agentless control plane with OKE's networks and storage classes; their pods move to agent nodes and their existing Services keep their old addresses, as they keep servicelb.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
• kubectl Authentication: The kubeconfig is the real OKE token version 2.0.0 shape: its user runs oci ce cluster generate-token --cluster-id <ocid> --region <region>, and its cluster entry carries the k3s CA, so TLS is verified. k3s does not know these tokens, so it sends each one to floci-oci in a Kubernetes TokenReview (a token webhook meant for the k3s sidecar and unauthenticated like every /_floci-oci endpoint, at /_floci-oci/oke/token-webhook/<tenancy>/<cluster>, the same design as floci-aws EKS). The API server caches each verdict for 30 seconds.
  • What a token is: generate-token signs a bare GET https://containerengine.<region>.oraclecloud.com/cluster_request/<cluster-ocid> with the caller's OCI signer over date (request-target) host, copies the authorization and date headers into the URL's query and base64url-encodes the URL (oci-cli containerengine_cli_extended.py, oci-python-sdk signer.py). The query is not part of what was signed.
  • What every mode checks: the token must be that URL for this cluster and its region, with an rsa-sha256 Signature over date (request-target) host, a keyId (or, for a session token, a tenant claim) in the cluster's tenancy, and a date within 5 minutes of now ("If the client's clock is skewed more than 5 minutes, a 401 (NotAuthenticated) HTTP status code is returned", Request Signatures).
  • Signature verification (FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_TOKEN_VERIFICATION):
Token signed with known-keys (default) strict off an API key uploaded to identity (UploadApiKey, Terraform oci_identity_api_key) signature verified against the key; the caller mapped as OKE maps IAM users (below); a bad signature is 401 same not verified; cluster-admin another key of a user who has uploaded keys 401 (OCI would not know the key) 401 not verified; cluster-admin a key of a user with no uploaded key not verified; cluster-admin, as before; a WARN once per key says how to change that 401 not verified; cluster-admin --auth security_token (ST$<jwt> keyId) for a user that exists in identity, with a jwk claim signature verified against the session key in jwk (proof the caller holds it), then mapped as OKE does; the JWT's own signature cannot be checked, since floci-oci issues no session tokens 401 not verified; cluster-admin any other session token, and instance principal tokens (ptype: instance) not verified; cluster-admin, username the token's sub (the instance OCID for an instance principal) 401 not verified; cluster-admin
  • Who a verified caller becomes: as OKE documents it ("A user's permissions to access clusters comes from the IAM groups ... to which they belong", "You can use OCIDs to map Kubernetes RBAC rolebindings and clusterrolebindings to IAM users and groups", "By default, users are not assigned any Kubernetes RBAC roles", About Access Control and Kubernetes Engine): the username and uid are the user's OCID, and the groups are the OCIDs of the user's IAM groups in the cluster's tenancy, then system:authenticated. A caller who holds manage on clusters where the cluster is also gets system:masters ("Oracle Cloud Infrastructure tenancy administrators already have sufficient privileges, and do not require the cluster-admin clusterrole", same page; AdministerK8s needs CLUSTER_MANAGE, Container Engine policy reference). That holds for a member of the tenancy's group named Administrators, or of a group that a policy of the cluster's tenancy lets manage clusters, manage cluster-family or manage all-resources in the cluster's compartment, one above it, or the tenancy. Anyone else has only what RBAC binds to User <user OCID> or Group <group OCID>, for example kubectl create rolebinding devs-view --clusterrole=view --group=<group OCID>. Verified callers also carry the extra fields seen on real clusters: AuthType=[Native], ContextType=[OCI], Principal=[<OCID>], TenancyID=[<OCID>], TokenV2=[true].
  • Becoming cluster-admin after uploading a key: floci-oci's default tenancy has no Administrators group (every real tenancy has one; floci-oci creates it only for child tenancies, through CreateChildTenancy). So a user who uploads its key goes from cluster-admin to 403 on everything, as a real non-administrator would, until it joins a group named Administrators (create it) or one of its groups gets a policy such as Allow group <name> to manage cluster-family in tenancy. floci-oci logs this the first time a verified user is not an administrator.
  • How policies are read: only Allow <subject> to manage <clusters | cluster-family | all-resources> in <location> statements count, where the subject is group <name>[, <name>], group id <ocid>[, id <ocid>], group '<domain>'/'<name>' (the Default domain only), any-group or any-user, and the location is tenancy (in a policy attached to the tenancy), compartment id <ocid>, or compartment <name>[:<name>] resolved from the compartment the policy is attached to (Policy Syntax, Policies and Compartment Hierarchies). Group and compartment names match ignoring case. A statement with a where clause never grants, nor does any other form floci-oci cannot evaluate (Endorse, Admit, permission lists, dynamic groups), so a policy can only make floci-oci stricter than OKE, never looser. Policies of other tenancies are never read, as only callers from the cluster's own tenancy are accepted.
  • Static token alternative: Each cluster also gets a random API token, stored with the cluster and never returned by CreateCluster, GetCluster or ListClusters. Set FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_KUBECONFIG_AUTH=token to receive it in the kubeconfig instead of the exec user, for clients without the oci CLI. It is cluster-admin on that cluster.
  • Prerequisites for kubectl: the oci CLI on PATH with a config whose key can sign. With known-keys, any key works until it is uploaded; with strict, upload it first (oci iam user api-key upload --user-id <ocid> --key-file <public.pem>).
  • Not verified against real OKE: OKE's token webhook is closed source and no Oracle page describes its algorithm. That it is OCI's standard signed-request check on GET /cluster_request/<cluster> is an inference from the token's shape; OKE's accepted clock window and whether it caches verdicts are not documented, so the 5 minutes is OCI's generic limit (generate-token refreshes after 4). The group list (system:masters for manage clusters holders, the order of the entries) and the extra keys come from third-party kubectl auth whoami output, not Oracle documentation. Whether OKE lists dynamic group OCIDs for users, and whether instance principal tokens carry a jwk claim, is not known.

docs.title: Persistence, mock mode and teardown
docs.text:
• Storage Persistence: each server keeps its state in a Docker named volume mounted at /var/lib/rancher/k3s, each agent in its own, and the oci storage class in a cluster-wide one, all obeying the global storage persistence and prune-volumes-on-delete policies.
  • Mock Mode: Setting FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_OKE_MOCK=true (default in test profiles) bypasses Docker: clusters are ACTIVE at once with the same endpoints a real cluster advertises on the default port (https://127.0.0.1:6443, private endpoint 10.0.0.10:6443), node pools list their nodes ACTIVE, and add-ons are recorded only.
  • Teardown: DELETE and application shutdown remove the k3s server and agent containers and the cluster network and keep or drop the named volumes by the policy above, so a persistent cluster comes back after a restart. POST /_floci-oci/state/reset forgets every cluster and so always removes its volume too, whatever prune-volumes-on-delete says. The anonymous volumes the k3s image declares always go with the container.

docs.title: Wire & Behavior Notes
docs.text:
• Kubeconfig Generation: POST /20180222/clusters/{id}/kubeconfig/content accepts the SDK's CreateClusterKubeconfigContentDetails (tokenVersion, expiration, endpoint). expiration is deprecated in the SDK and ignored. endpoint must be one of LEGACY_KUBERNETES, PUBLIC_ENDPOINT, PRIVATE_ENDPOINT or VCN_HOSTNAME (any case; otherwise 400 InvalidParameter); floci-oci has one reachable API address, https://127.0.0.1:{hostPort}, so every value resolves to it. Which endpoint real OKE picks when endpoint is omitted is not stated in the SDKs or the CLI (both leave it optional with no default), so that case resolves to the same address. Before the cluster is ACTIVE (or in mock mode) there is no CA yet, and the kubeconfig falls back to insecure-skip-tls-verify: true.
  • Cluster settings read back as sent: type, endpointConfig, options, imagePolicyConfig and clusterPodNetworkOptions are stored from CreateClusterDetails and returned by GetCluster and ListClusters exactly as given, reduced to the fields of their SDK types. Nothing is filled in for a setting that was not sent, since the defaults real OKE applies are not documented in the SDKs. Enum values (type, cniType, ipFamilies) are checked (400 InvalidParameter). Apart from options.kubernetesNetworkConfig (see Networking) and type (which gates add-ons), they are management-plane only: the k3s server does not change with them. systemTags is always {}.
  • Cluster updates: UpdateCluster changes the name, version, tags, type, imagePolicyConfig, and the options UpdateClusterOptionsDetails allows (admissionControllerOptions, persistentVolumeConfig, serviceLbConfig, OpenID Connect); the network options set on create stay. UpdateClusterEndpointConfig changes the NSGs, public IP and security attributes and keeps the subnet; ClusterMigrateToNativeVcn gives a cluster created without one its endpointConfig (what Terraform calls when endpoint_config is added later). Both answer 202 with a CLUSTER_UPDATE work request. GetCluster returns an etag, which if-match on these three operations checks.
  • Public endpoint: with endpointConfig.isPublicIpEnabled true, endpoints.publicEndpoint is the cluster's one reachable address, as host:port.
  • Work Requests: Asynchronous mutations (such as cluster and node pool creation or deletion) return 202 Accepted with an opc-work-request-id header, pollable via /20180222/workRequests/{id}. CreateCluster and CreateNodePool return no body, as in the SDK: the new resource's OCID is the work request's resources[0].identifier. A cluster create that fails (the k3s sidecar exits, or is not ready in time) leaves its reason both in the cluster's lifecycleDetails and as an InternalServerError entry of ListWorkRequestErrors, which is where Terraform reads it.
  • Node pools need an ACTIVE cluster: on a CREATING cluster CreateNodePool is 409 IncorrectState (which SDKs retry), and on a FAILED, DELETING or DELETED one it is 409 Conflict. OCI documents neither case, so both are floci-oci's choice. GetNodePool and ListNodePools always carry systemTags {}, as the cluster does, so the oracle/oci provider (9.12 and later) plans no drift after an apply.
  • Node pool fields: nodeConfigDetails, subnetIds, nodeShapeConfig, initialNodeLabels, nodeSourceDetails, sshPublicKey, nodeMetadata, nodePoolCyclingDetails and nodeEvictionNodePoolSettings are stored as sent, reduced to the fields of their SDK types, and nodes[] lists one node per requested node with its OCID, name, availability domain, fault domain, subnet, private IP, Kubernetes version and lifecycle state. nodeSourceDetails, sshPublicKey, nodeMetadata and the eviction settings have no runtime effect.
  • Immutable Container Naming: Sidecar containers are named using the immutable cluster OCID (floci-oci-oke-ocid1.cluster.oc1.iad.xxx), ensuring display name updates via UpdateCluster do not affect container lifecycle or teardown.

docs.title: What floci-oci decides where Oracle is silent
docs.text:
• How a token is verified (OCI's signed-request check, inferred), the 5-minute window, and which callers are verified in each token-verification mode.

  • The load balancer address ranges, which end of the node subnet internal load balancers take, and the order of a public NLB's two addresses.

  • Error codes for an invalid initialNodeLabels entry, an invalid or overlapping kubernetesNetworkConfig, a node pool on a cluster that is not ACTIVE, an unknown, duplicate or dependent add-on, and add-ons on a basic cluster.

  • The default memory per OCPU of a flexible shape when nodeShapeConfig sets only the OCPUs, and the size of a shape outside the catalog.
  • INSTANCE_REPLACE as the default cycle mode, and replacing every node at once.
  • The node labels Oracle does not document (displayName, hostname, internal_addr, name, node.info/*), which part of each OCID goes into a node name (the last ten characters), and the kube-dns address in a non-default service network.
  • Which add-on versions ListAddonOptions reports.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
E="--endpoint http://localhost:4599"
TENANCY=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..flocilocaltenancy0000000000000000000000000000000000000000

# Create a cluster (enhanced, so it takes add-ons)
oci ce cluster create $E --compartment-id "$TENANCY" \
  --name demo-cluster --vcn-id "ocid1.vcn.oc1.iad.demovcn" --kubernetes-version "v1.36.4" --type ENHANCED_CLUSTER

# List clusters
oci ce cluster list $E --compartment-id "$TENANCY"

# Add two worker nodes (real mode: two k3s agents)
oci ce node-pool create $E --compartment-id "$TENANCY" --cluster-id "ocid1.cluster.oc1.iad.demo" \
  --name workers --node-shape VM.Standard.E4.Flex --node-shape-config '{"ocpus": 1, "memoryInGBs": 4}' \
  --size 2 --placement-configs '[{"availabilityDomain": "Floc:US-ASHBURN-AD-1", "subnetId": "ocid1.subnet.oc1.iad.workers"}]'

# Download kubeconfig (once the cluster is ACTIVE, so it carries the CA)
oci ce cluster create-kubeconfig $E --cluster-id "ocid1.cluster.oc1.iad.demo" --file ./kubeconfig

# kubectl runs `oci ce cluster generate-token` for each request; real mode only
KUBECONFIG=./kubeconfig kubectl get nodes

# A LoadBalancer Service gets an OCI-shaped address and a port on 127.0.0.1
KUBECONFIG=./kubeconfig kubectl expose deployment web --type=LoadBalancer --port=80 --target-port=8080
KUBECONFIG=./kubeconfig kubectl get service web \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip} {.metadata.annotations.floci\.io/load-balancer-host-ports}'

# kubectl top needs the metrics server add-on, as on OKE
oci ce cluster install-addon $E --cluster-id "ocid1.cluster.oc1.iad.demo" --addon-name CertManager
oci ce cluster install-addon $E --cluster-id "ocid1.cluster.oc1.iad.demo" --addon-name KubernetesMetricsServer

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: OCI Functions, on API versions 20260325 (every current SDK and OCI CLI 3.94) and 20181201 (older SDKs, the fn CLI and fn_go). This is floci-oci's Docker-sidecar reference service: the management plane is emulated in-process, and real invocations run your function image through a shared Fn Project server — the same open-source engine OCI Functions is built on.

docs.title: Supported operations
docs.text: Area Operations Applications Create, Get, List, Update, Delete, ChangeCompartment Functions Create, Get, List, Update, Delete Invocation InvokeFunction (sync, detached, is-dry-run) Work requests (20260325) GetWorkRequest, ListWorkRequests, ListWorkRequestErrors, ListWorkRequestLogs, CancelWorkRequest Catalogs (20260325) ListFunctionsRuntimes, GetFunctionsRuntime, ListFunctionsRuntimeVersions, GetFunctionsRuntimeVersion, ListPbfListings, GetPbfListing, ListPbfListingVersions, GetPbfListingVersion, ListTriggers

docs.title: Two API versions
docs.text:
Both versions serve the same applications and functions, so a function created through one is visible through the other. They differ where the SDKs differ:

20181201 20260325 Create 200, body, etag 200, body, etag, opc-work-request-id Update, Delete, ChangeCompartment 200 with body (204 for delete) 202, no body, opc-work-request-id A function's image top-level image, imageDigest sourceDetails {sourceType: CONTAINER_IMAGE, image, imageDigest}
  • The SDKs declare no status codes; 202 for the operations that answer with only a work request is floci-oci's choice, as in its other services.
  • Every mutation finishes before it returns, so its work request is SUCCEEDED with timeFinished set, which is what Terraform's waiters poll for. Resources are reported as functionsApplication and functionsFunction, which contain the substrings Terraform matches. Errors and logs are always empty, and cancel is 409 Conflict. A change-compartment reports UPDATE_APPLICATION: the SDK has no operation type of its own for it.
  • sourceDetails must be CONTAINER_IMAGE: fnserver runs container images only, so ARCHIVE and PRE_BUILT_FUNCTIONS are 501 MethodNotImplemented. A digest sent with the image is kept; otherwise one is derived.
  • The runtime catalog holds java17.ol9 and python312.ol9, names taken from the OCI CLI's tests; their other values are floci-oci's. No pre-built functions are listed.
  • The optional settings (an application's networkSecurityGroupIds, syslogUrl, traceConfig, logging, imagePolicyConfig, securityAttributes; a function's provisionedConcurrencyConfig, detachedModeTimeoutInSeconds, failureDestination, successDestination, traceConfig) are accepted on both versions and returned as sent. They do not change how a function runs.

docs.title: Wire notes
docs.text:
• On 20181201 there are no work requests: Functions is synchronous with lifecycle-state polling.
  • Lists are bare JSON arrays; ListFunctions requires applicationId.
  • Exact casing matters: memoryInMBs.
  • imageDigest is deterministic per image and changes when the image changes — Terraform's CustomizeDiff depends on this, otherwise plans drift forever.
  • invokeEndpoint is a stable host-only base URL; invocation is raw binary in, binary out — never JSON-wrapped by the emulator.
  • Deleting an application with functions still in it is a 409.

docs.title: Mock mode vs real invocation
docs.text:
floci-oci.services.functions.mock Behaviour false (default) Starts a shared fnproject/fnserver container on first invoke, mirrors the app/function into it, and proxies the call to the real image true No Docker at all; the management plane works fully and invocations return a synthetic body

The test suite sets mock: true so it never needs Docker.

# Disable the sidecar entirely
FLOCI_OCI_SERVICES_FUNCTIONS_MOCK=true

Real invocation requires the Docker socket — the emulator's container mounts it, and fnserver spawns your function containers as siblings.

docs.text:
E="--endpoint http://localhost:4599"
TENANCY=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..flocilocaltenancy0000000000000000000000000000000000000000

oci fn application create $E --compartment-id "$TENANCY" \
  --display-name demo-app --subnet-ids '["ocid1.subnet.oc1.iad.demo"]'
oci fn function create $E --application-id <appId> --display-name hello \
  --image <your-fdk-image>:latest --memory-in-mbs 128
oci fn function invoke $E --function-id <fnId> --body '{"name":"floci"}' --file -

docs.title: Notes & limitations
docs.text:
• Your image must be a current FDK build (http-stream contract). Older fnproject/hello images predate it and fail to initialize.
  • Pre-built functions and archive sources are not runnable (501), provisioned concurrency, trace configs and destinations are recorded only, and detached-invocation results are not tracked.
  • fn-invoke-type: detached returns 202 immediately and runs the function in the background; is-dry-run: true validates without executing.

docs.title: Governance Rules
docs.text: The OCI Governance Rules control plane, API version 20220504. A parent tenancy defines rules for the child tenancies of its organization: quotas, tags or the regions children may use. Inclusion criteria pick the children a rule applies to, and a tenancy attachment records the rule applied to one child. Real OCI serves it on governance-rules.organizations.{region}.oci.{domain}; floci-oci serves it on port 4599 with the other services.

docs.title: Supported operations
docs.text: Area Operations Governance rules CreateGovernanceRule, GetGovernanceRule, ListGovernanceRules, UpdateGovernanceRule, DeleteGovernanceRule, RetryGovernanceRule Inclusion criteria CreateInclusionCriterion, GetInclusionCriterion, ListInclusionCriteria, DeleteInclusionCriterion Tenancy attachments GetTenancyAttachment, ListTenancyAttachments, RetryTenancyAttachment Enforced governance rules GetEnforcedGovernanceRule, ListEnforcedGovernanceRules Work requests GetWorkRequest, ListWorkRequests, CancelWorkRequest, ListWorkRequestErrors, ListWorkRequestLogs (/20220504/workRequests)

docs.title: Wire notes
docs.text:
• CreateGovernanceRule and CreateInclusionCriterion return 200 with the resource, an etag, an opc-work-request-id and a location header. Update, delete and both retries return 202 with an opc-work-request-id and no body. Every work request is already SUCCEEDED.
  • Lists are wrapped ({"items":[…]}) and paged with opc-next-page. Summaries leave out the template. sortBy takes timeCreated or displayName, sortOrder ASC or DESC.
  • ListGovernanceRules and ListTenancyAttachments need compartmentId or governanceRuleId (400 MissingParameter otherwise), as the SDK documents; ListInclusionCriteria needs governanceRuleId.
  • The template is polymorphic on type: ALLOWED_REGIONS needs displayName and regions (known region names), QUOTA needs displayName and statements, TAG needs name. A template whose type differs from the rule's is 400 InvalidParameter.
  • Rules are created in the root compartment (the tenancy OCID) of a tenancy that is not a child. Another compartment is 400 InvalidParameter.
  • CancelWorkRequest on a finished work request, and changing a DELETED rule or inclusion criterion, are 409 Conflict.
  • GetEnforcedGovernanceRule returns an etag that changes whenever the rule is edited or its tenancy attachment changes.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text:
ALLOWED_REGIONS is enforced: a child governed by such a rule cannot subscribe to a region outside its list. CreateRegionSubscription answers 400 InvalidParameter and names the rule. A child is governed when it is an ACTIVE member of the organization, its governanceStatus is OPTED_IN (see AddGovernance and RemoveGovernance in Organizations), and an active inclusion criterion of the rule covers it (ALL, or TENANCY naming it).

QUOTA and TAG rules are stored, attached and listed as enforced rules, but have no effect: floci-oci has no quotas or tagging service to apply them to.

docs.title: Emulator choices
docs.text:
The SDKs give the shapes but not the behaviour, so floci-oci picks:

  • Data is global, like Organizations: rules, criteria and attachments are kept with the parent tenancy and seen from every region.
  • Tenancy attachments are kept in step with the rules: a child that becomes governed gets an ACTIVE attachment, and one that stops being governed (it opts out, leaves, or the rule or criterion is deleted) has its attachment set to DELETED.
  • Deleting a rule sets it and its inclusion criteria to DELETED; they can still be read.
  • An enforced governance rule is the child's view of one attachment: its compartmentId is the child tenancy, and only the child can read it.
  • OCIDs: ocid1.governancerule…, ocid1.inclusioncriterion…, ocid1.tenancyattachment…, ocid1.enforcedgovernancerule….
  • The corpus does not say how real OCI enforces ALLOWED_REGIONS or which error it returns; refusing the region subscription with 400 InvalidParameter is floci-oci's choice.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
E="--endpoint http://localhost:4599"
TENANCY=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..flocilocaltenancy0000000000000000000000000000000000000000

oci governance-rules-control-plane governance-rule create-governance-rule-allowed-regions-template $E \
  --compartment-id "$TENANCY" --display-name only-ashburn --type ALLOWED_REGIONS --creation-option TEMPLATE \
  --template-display-name only-ashburn --template-regions '["us-ashburn-1"]'
oci governance-rules-control-plane governance-rule list $E --compartment-id "$TENANCY"

docs.title: Identity (IAM)
docs.text: OCI Identity and Access Management — API version 20160918.

docs.title: Supported operations
docs.text: Resource Operations Compartments Create, Get, List (compartmentIdInSubtree, name, lifecycleState, sortBy, sortOrder, accessLevel), Update, Delete and Move (async, work request), Recover Users Create, Get, List, Update, Delete API signing keys UploadApiKey, ListApiKeys, DeleteApiKey Groups Create, Get, List, Update, Delete User group memberships AddUserToGroup, Get, List (by user/group), RemoveUserFromGroup Policies Create, Get, List, Update, Delete Availability domains List (3 ADs) Fault domains List (3 per AD) Regions List (every region in the realm of the request's region) Region subscriptions List, Create Tenancies Get Work requests Get, List

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
TENANCY=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..flocilocaltenancy0000000000000000000000000000000000000000

oci iam compartment create --endpoint http://localhost:4599 \
  --compartment-id "$TENANCY" --name dev --description "Development"

oci iam compartment list --endpoint http://localhost:4599 --compartment-id "$TENANCY"

docs.title: Notes & limitations
docs.text:
• The root compartment is the tenancy itself; GET /compartments/{tenancyOcid} returns it.
  • Deleting a compartment is asynchronous, like real OCI: 202 + opc-work-request-id. The compartment must be empty, in every region: no child compartments, no policies, and no resources of any other service (buckets, queues, streams, vaults, keys, secrets, functions applications, OKE clusters and node pools). If anything is left, the work request ends FAILED with a Conflict error listing it, and the compartment stays ACTIVE. Otherwise it ends SUCCEEDED and the compartment is DELETED with a random suffix appended to its name (dev.qR5hP2BD), which RecoverCompartment keeps. Deleting a DELETED compartment again succeeds and leaves it unchanged. The work request finishes immediately (real OCI takes a few minutes and passes through DELETING).
  • Compartments nest at most six levels below the tenancy, and a tenancy holds at most 1,000 compartments that are not DELETED, as on real OCI. OCI documents both limits but not their errors, so the codes are emulator choices: creating, moving or recovering a compartment past the depth limit is 400 InvalidParameter, and the count limit is 400 LimitExceeded with a message that starts "Maximum number of compartments", the text the Terraform provider looks for.
  • Availability domains follow the real naming, <prefix>:<region>-AD-<n>: the prefix is Floc for the default tenancy and a stable four letters derived from the OCID for any other, and the region part is PHX and US-ASHBURN for the two original regions and the upper-cased region name elsewhere (Floc:US-ASHBURN-AD-1, Floc:PHX-AD-1, Floc:US-CHICAGO-1-AD-1). Fault domains are FAULT-DOMAIN-1 to FAULT-DOMAIN-3.
  • compartmentIdInSubtree=true is only accepted on the tenancy (root compartment), as on real OCI. accessLevel is validated but not enforced: every compartment is accessible.
  • Region subscriptions complete immediately with status READY. Each tenancy has its own home region, reported by GetTenancy as homeRegionKey: a tenancy seen for the first time gets default-region and keeps it, so changing default-region later does not move an existing tenancy's home.
  • A tenancy can only use the regions it is subscribed to, as on real OCI: a request whose Host names another region returns 401 NotAuthenticated. The home region is always subscribed, and CreateRegionSubscription adds one more at once, so a multi-region setup needs that one call per extra region (by hand or from an init hook). A region outside the tenancy's realm is rejected the same way; OCI documents that rule but not its error code, so the 401 there is an emulator choice. A Host that names no region (localhost) always reaches the tenancy's home region. Emulator endpoints, pre-authenticated requests and CreateRegionSubscription itself are never blocked.
  • Every other service requires its compartmentId to be an ACTIVE compartment created here, or the tenancy itself (the root compartment), as on real OCI: an unknown, deleted or blank one is 400 RelatedResourceNotAuthorizedOrNotFound in a request body and 404 NotAuthorizedOrNotFound in a query. Create the compartment first, or use the tenancy OCID. The check is skipped only when Identity is disabled, since nothing could then create a compartment.
  • As on real OCI, compartments, users, groups, group memberships and policies can only be created, updated or deleted through the home region's endpoint. A write sent with another region in the Host header returns 403 NotAllowed ("This operation must be directed at the home region."). Reads work in every region, and changes are visible everywhere at once (real OCI takes a few minutes to propagate them). Clients that never set a region host reach their tenancy's home region, so they are unaffected. CreateRegionSubscription is accepted in every region: the SDKs do not tie it to the home region, so floci-oci does not either.
  • Policy statements are stored verbatim and never enforced on API calls. The one place floci-oci reads them is OKE's token webhook, which looks for manage grants on clusters to decide who is a cluster administrator (see the Container Engine page, "Authentication").
  • API signing keys (/20160918/users/{userId}/apiKeys): UploadApiKey takes {"key": "<PEM>"}, an RSA public key of at least 2048 bits ("RSA key pair in PEM format (minimum 2048 bits)", Required Keys and OCIDs), and returns the ApiKey with its fingerprint (the colon-separated MD5 of the DER public key, the value openssl rsa -pubout -outform DER | openssl md5 -c prints) and its keyId <tenancy>/<user>/<fingerprint>. A user holds at most three keys ("You can have up to three API key pairs per user", same page). The key is ACTIVE at once (OCI: briefly CREATING). ListApiKeys returns a bare array; DeleteApiKey takes the fingerprint and answers 204. Deleting a user deletes its keys. Request signatures on the API itself are still parsed and never verified: an uploaded key only matters to OKE's token webhook, which verifies the oci ce cluster generate-token tokens signed with it.
  • Identity domains, auth tokens, customer secret keys, dynamic groups and tag namespaces are not implemented yet.

docs.title: Emulator choices
docs.text:
Behaviour that OCI's SDKs and documentation do not settle, and what floci-oci does:

  • Compartment names are unique per parent. The SDK's CreateCompartment comment says a name must be unique across the tenancy, while the compartments documentation says two compartments within the same parent can't share a name. floci-oci follows the documentation.
  • MoveCompartment work requests use operation type MOVE_COMPARTMENT. Identity's WorkRequest enum only lists DELETE_COMPARTMENT and DELETE_TAG_DEFINITION.
  • ListRegions lists the regions of the request's realm, the realm of the region named by the Host header (or the home region), since a tenancy can only use regions in its realm.
  • Changes are immediate. Region subscriptions are READY at once (OCI: IN_PROGRESS for several minutes), IAM changes are visible in every region at once (OCI: a few minutes to propagate from the home region), and compartment delete and move work requests finish at once.
  • Error codes OCI does not document for a rule it does document: 400 InvalidParameter for the compartment depth limit, 400 LimitExceeded for the compartment count limit, 401 NotAuthenticated for a region outside the realm, and a Conflict work-request error for a non-empty compartment. For API keys, not verified against real OCI: 400 InvalidParameter for a fourth key and for a key that is not RSA, is shorter than 2048 bits or is not PEM, and 409 Conflict for a key the user already has.

docs.title: Vault, KMS and Secrets
docs.text:
Three OCI services that work together:

Service API SDK client KMS vaults /20180608/vaults KmsVaultClient KMS keys /20180608/keys KmsManagementClient KMS crypto /20180608/{encrypt,decrypt,…} KmsCryptoClient Secrets (management) /20180608/secrets VaultsClient Secrets (retrieval) /20190301/secretbundles SecretsClient

docs.title: Supported operations
docs.text: Area Operations Vaults Create, Get, List, Update, ScheduleDeletion, CancelDeletion, ChangeCompartment Keys Create, Get, List, Update, Enable, Disable, ScheduleDeletion, CancelDeletion, Import (AES, RSA) Wrapping key GetWrappingKey Key versions Create (rotate), Import, Get, List Crypto Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataEncryptionKey, Sign, Verify Secrets CreateSecret, GetSecret, ListSecrets, UpdateSecret, Schedule/CancelDeletion, versions Bundles GetSecretBundle, GetSecretBundleByName, ListSecretBundleVersions

docs.title: Real cryptography
docs.text:
Crypto is not stubbed. Keys hold real material:

  • AES — AES-GCM encrypt/decrypt. The ciphertext envelope carries the key-version id, so ciphertext produced before a rotation still decrypts afterwards.
  • RSA / ECDSA — real JCA sign/verify (SHA_*_RSA_PKCS1_V1_5, ECDSA_SHA_*).
  • plaintextChecksum (CRC32) is returned on Decrypt and GenerateDataEncryptionKey, as the wire contract requires.

docs.title: Wire notes
docs.text:
• There is no DELETE verb for vaults, keys or secrets — deletion is scheduled via actions/scheduleDeletion and reflected in lifecycleState (PENDING_DELETION), reversible with actions/cancelDeletion.
  • Keys reach ENABLED, not ACTIVE.
  • KeySummary has no keyShape/currentKeyVersion but carries a flat algorithm.
  • The Secret shape never echoes content — content is only readable through a secret bundle.
  • GetSecretBundleByName is a POST with query parameters, no body, and no etag.
  • Single secret versions live at /version/{n} (singular); the list is /versions.

docs.title: Endpoint indirection (deviation)
docs.text:
Real OCI gives each vault its own management/crypto hostname, returned as managementEndpoint / cryptoEndpoint. The OCI SDKs reject endpoints containing a path (endpoint must not contain user info, path, query, or fragment), so the emulator cannot encode the vault in a path suffix and returns its own host for both.

Consequence: CreateKey carries no vaultId, so a new key is attached to the caller's compartment vault — the most recently created ACTIVE one. With the usual one-vault setup this is exact; with several vaults in one compartment, keys land in the newest.

docs.title: Key import
docs.text:
GetWrappingKey returns a real RSA-4096 public key in PEM form. ImportKey unwraps the supplied wrappedImportKey.keyMaterial with its private half and stores the material as the key's first version, with origin EXTERNAL. ImportKeyVersion does the same for an existing key and makes the new version current, as CreateKeyVersion does. Imported keys then work with every crypto operation.

  • RSA_OAEP_SHA256: the material encrypted directly with RSA-OAEP (SHA-256 digest and MGF1).
  • RSA_OAEP_AES_SHA256: a temporary AES key encrypted with RSA-OAEP, followed by the material wrapped with that AES key (AES key wrap with padding, RFC 5649).
Key Lengths (keyShape.length, bytes) Material Wrapping AES 16, 24, 32 the raw key, exactly that many bytes RSA_OAEP_SHA256 or RSA_OAEP_AES_SHA256 RSA 256, 384, 512 the DER PKCS8 private key; the public key is derived from it RSA_OAEP_AES_SHA256 only

As in OCI, ECDSA keys can't be imported: ImportKey and ImportKeyVersion reject them with 400 InvalidParameter.

One wrapping key pair for every vault (deviation). Real OCI keeps a wrapping key per vault and picks the vault from the request hostname. GetWrappingKey carries no vault id and every vault shares the emulator host, so every vault keeps its own wrappingkeyId but they all share one RSA key pair. GetWrappingKey reports the most recently created ACTIVE vault, with that vault's wrappingkeyId as its id. The key pair is generated on first use and kept in the kms storage, so it survives restarts in persistent modes.

docs.text:
E="--endpoint http://localhost:4599"
TENANCY=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..flocilocaltenancy0000000000000000000000000000000000000000

oci kms management vault create $E --compartment-id "$TENANCY" \
  --display-name demo-vault --vault-type DEFAULT

docs.title: Notes & limitations
docs.text: Key backup/restore, vault replication, external key managers, secret rotation configs and secret rules are not implemented.

docs.title: Object Storage

docs.text:

E="--endpoint http://localhost:4599"

oci os bucket create $E --compartment-id "$TENANCY" --namespace floci-local --name demo

docs.title: Notes & limitations
docs.text:
• Each tenancy has its own namespace, the same in every region, as on real OCI. The default tenancy (unsigned requests, or default-tenancy-id) uses floci-oci.default-namespace (default floci-local); any other signing tenancy gets a stable 12 character namespace derived from its OCID. GetNamespace returns the caller's, and with ?compartmentId=<tenancy OCID> that tenancy's (a compartment OCID resolves to the caller's namespace).
  • A namespace in the path that is not the caller's is answered with 404 NamespaceNotFound, as on real OCI. Ask GetNamespace for the namespace instead of hard-coding one.
  • Pre-authenticated request URLs work for every tenancy: the token is looked up across tenancies in the request's region, must match the namespace in the URL, and acts as the tenancy that created it.
  • CopyObject honours destinationRegion (required, as on real OCI): the destination bucket must exist in that region and the copy lands there. The copy completes immediately; its work request (COMPLETED) is read from the source region.
  • Content-MD5 is verified on upload; opc-content-md5 is returned.
  • CommitMultipartUpload returns opc-multipart-md5: the Base64 MD5 of the committed parts' binary MD5 digests in part-number order, followed by - and the part count. GetObject and HeadObject return the same value for multipart objects, in place of content-md5.
  • Object versioning, retention rules, lifecycle policies, replication and the Amazon S3 Compatibility API are not implemented yet.

docs.title: Organizations
docs.text: OCI Organizations (the Tenant Manager control plane), API version 20230401. A parent tenancy creates child tenancies; together they form an organization, and each child is linked to the parent per feature. Real OCI serves it on organizations.{region}.oci.{domain}; floci-oci serves it on port 4599 with the other services.
